items.text: Confirmed mismatch M1 (noLock conflated with acceptance bypass) at the exact code site: scenarios/workspace-sandbox/api/internal/sandbox/service.go:1146-1147 has the explicit comment 'When noLock is true, all files are automatically accepted (no acceptance rules apply)'. This now anchors Finding 4 M1 and the description rewrite for fix/workspace-sandbox-lock-and-acceptance-semantics.

Confirmed the env-var contract: VROOLI_SANDBOX_ID, VROOLI_SANDBOX_MERGED, VROOLI_SANDBOX_SCOPE are emitted by scenarios/agent-manager/api/internal/orchestration/run_executor.go (around lines 1155-1163) and consumed by internal/scenario/scenario.go, internal/scenarioexec/subprocess.go, internal/cli/vroolicli/runtime.go, and internal/repocontractcheck/checks.go. The agent never sees these vars in its prompt; they are propagated transparently into subprocesses via scenarioexec. This satisfies the 'transparent to agent' contract requirement.

Resolved the stale-path question (round-1 d6=A). The canonical scenario-restart and lifecycle code is Go in internal/, not bash in scripts/lib/scenario/ or cli/commands/scenario/. The TeardownHooks documentation in workspace-sandbox/api/internal/config/config.go:225 already references 'vrooli scenario heal-from-sandbox' (the Go CLI), confirming the migration. This research's own acceptance_allow needs updating, and so does the initiative context document.

The current GCT provenance schema (scenarios/git-control-tower/api/approved_changes_model.go) has no field for run outcome. ProvenanceRunGroup carries runId, sandboxId, sandboxOwner, files[], latestAppliedAt — but no runOutcome, fromFailedRun, or runStatus. Round-1 d3=A locks 'identical apply behavior; record run outcome in provenance metadata so GCT can render differently' — which means this research's actions must require the schema to grow a runOutcome field. Round-2 d1 below pins the precise shape.

items.topic: Provenance schema: where does run outcome live?
items.context: Round-1 d3=A locked 'apply identically regardless of outcome; record run outcome in provenance metadata so GCT can render differently.' The current ProvenanceRunGroup has no outcome field. The contract needs to specify (a) where the field lives in the schema, and (b) what its value space is. Three reasonable shapes: extend ProvenanceRunGroup with a single enum field (smallest surface); add a richer RunMetadata sub-object (extensible for future fields like cost, conversation_id, model); or attach outcome to each ProvenanceFile (allows per-file outcome but loses run-level rollup).

options.label: Extend ProvenanceRunGroup with a single field: runOutcome enum {success, failure, cancelled, timeout}
options.rationale: Minimal schema change; matches GCT's existing per-run grouping; 'cancelled' and 'timeout' are useful operator distinctions beyond binary success/failure

options.label: Add a RunMetadata sub-object to ProvenanceRunGroup containing runOutcome plus costUsd, conversationId, modelId, durationMs
options.rationale: Future-proofs the schema for the broader 'audit trail' vision (cost, conversation, model attribution); larger surface and forces multi-step shape negotiation now

options.label: Binary boolean: ProvenanceRunGroup.runFailed bool (true if any non-success outcome)
options.rationale: Smallest possible change; loses the success/cancelled/timeout distinction that Finding 5.2 implies operators care about

items.context: Initiative pre-decided manualReview is opt-in. But when an operator opts in, what changes? Two coherent interpretations: (A) auto-apply still runs at run end, but the resulting commit is held in a 'pending operator review' state in GCT before being merged/pushed; (B) auto-apply does NOT run at run end — sandbox changes wait until the operator clicks Approve in the AI Changes tab, at which point apply executes. (A) keeps the apply path uniform between modes (always applies at run end, review gates downstream); (B) makes manual review a true gate on apply itself. The choice affects the contract's state machine: in (A) the sandbox can be torn down right after apply; in (B) the sandbox must persist until operator action.

options.label: Auto-apply at run end is uniform across modes; manualReview gates the downstream commit/push step in GCT, not apply
options.rationale: Uniform apply path simplifies the contract; sandbox can teardown immediately; matches the 'auditability-first' framing where applied changes are always recorded even if humans haven't blessed them yet

options.label: manualReview=true defers apply until operator approves in GCT; sandbox persists until then
options.rationale: Makes manual review a true safety gate on the canonical repo; matches operator intuition for 'manual review' but complicates sandbox lifecycle (must persist beyond run end) and contradicts the unified state machine

items.notes: Note that operator should be able to approve from git-control-tower, agent-manager, or workspace-sandbox. They all are locations where a run’s diff can be viewed and a user might expect this behavior

items.topic: Sandbox creation timing: eager or lazy?
items.context: Should agent-manager create the sandbox at run start (eager — every coding run gets exactly one sandbox even if the agent never writes a file) or lazily on first write attempt (lazy — runs that produce no changes leave no sandbox)? Eager makes 'every coding run produces provenance' literally true and gives operators a uniform navigation experience in GCT (every run has an AI Changes entry, even if empty). Lazy reduces overhead and keeps GCT free of empty entries but means the audit trail has gaps for read-only/no-op runs. The bias of this initiative is auditability-first.

options.label: Eager: sandbox created at run start regardless of whether the agent writes anything; empty provenance records are fine
options.rationale: Uniform contract ('every run has provenance'); simpler reasoning; no race between agent first-write and sandbox readiness; matches auditability-first bias

options.label: Lazy: sandbox created on first write; no-op runs have no sandbox and no provenance entry
options.rationale: Lower resource use; cleaner GCT view (no empty entries); contradicts the literal reading of 'every coding run produces provenance' but arguably 'coding run' implies writes occurred

options.label: Eager but garbage-collect empty sandboxes within N seconds of run end
options.rationale: Compromise: uniform creation contract but tidy resource state. Adds GC complexity; provenance still exists in the audit trail

items.topic: Out-of-acceptance review-queue: which surface owns it?
items.context: Round-1 d5=B locked 'retain out-of-acceptance changes in the sandbox + surface them as a GCT review-queue entry the operator can manually approve to apply.' Two implementation shapes: (A) workspace-sandbox exposes a new endpoint that returns the out-of-acceptance set per sandbox/run; GCT calls it and renders the review queue; (B) workspace-sandbox writes a separate provenance category (e.g., 'pending-review') alongside applied provenance, and GCT just queries the existing provenance API with a filter. (A) is a cleaner separation of concerns; (B) reuses existing plumbing.

options.label: New workspace-sandbox endpoint: GET /sandboxes/{id}/out-of-acceptance-changes returns the held-back set; GCT polls per run and renders
options.rationale: Clean separation; explicit API contract; GCT doesn't need to know about provenance categories

options.label: Extend provenance with a 'state' field: state in {applied, pending-review, denied}; GCT filters the existing provenance API by state=pending-review
options.rationale: Reuses the existing GCT/workspace-sandbox plumbing (one schema, one endpoint); makes the audit trail uniform; pairs naturally with d1 if d1=A or B is chosen

items.topic: Validation matrix scope: which spawn surfaces gate the default flip?
items.context: Finding 5 lists eight behaviors that must work end-to-end. The remaining question is which spawn surfaces those behaviors must work across before sandboxing flips to default. Spawn surfaces in the codebase today: (1) agent-manager web UI manual run creation; (2) swarm-manager queue (auto-spawned runs from queued backlog items); (3) scheduled cron-spawned runs; (4) direct CLI invocation. Validating all four before flipping is the safest path but slows the rollout; validating only the high-traffic surfaces (1+2) accepts known gaps in 3+4.

options.label: All four spawn surfaces (UI, swarm-manager queue, cron, CLI) must pass Finding 5 before default flips
options.rationale: Most defensive; matches the 'as many runs as possible flow through sandboxing' goal; slowest path

options.label: UI + swarm-manager queue only (covering the high-volume surfaces); cron and CLI flip independently in follow-on items
options.rationale: Pragmatic: covers the surfaces operators actually use; cron and CLI are lower-volume and can ride the same default once the foundation is proven

options.label: UI only — minimal viable validation, all other surfaces follow individually
options.rationale: Fastest to default, but leaves the swarm-manager queue (the highest-volume coding-run source) un-validated at flip time

plan_updates: Synthesized round-1 answers (all 7 decisions resolved) into the conclusion: Finding 1 now contains the locked defaults table; Finding 2 has the preliminary config surface; Finding 3 is a fully populated source-of-truth matrix grounded in actual code paths (including the corrected internal/ Go locations); Finding 4 enumerates 5 mismatches with code-site evidence and routes each to a specific follow-on item; Finding 5 lists 8 validation behaviors; Finding 6 finalizes the sequencing. Actions section is now anticipated as 7 concrete actions covering 4 backlog-item updates, 1 self-update for stale paths, and 2 document mirrors. Round-2 decisions focus on the remaining contract details: provenance outcome schema (d1), apply timing under manualReview (d2), sandbox creation timing (d3), out-of-acceptance review-queue ownership (d4), and validation-matrix surface scope (d5).
